title: Shopping & numbers in context
blurb: Ask prices, judge whether something's a good deal, and handle a basic purchase.

vocab.example: Ten svetr stojí osm set korun.
Tady je to dost drahé, zkusíme jiný obchod.

vocab.translation: Do you have this in another size?
vocab.example: Máte tu bundu v jiné velikosti, prosím?

vocab.translation: to pay by card / in cash

vocab.example: Je na tenhle svetr nějaká sleva?

grammarNote.title: Counting nouns: 1 / 2–4 / 5+ take different endings
grammarNote.text: Numbers change the ending of the noun right after them, and Czech splits into three groups: 1 uses the plain dictionary form (jedna koruna), 2–4 use one ending (dvě koruny, tři koruny), and 5 and up use another (pět korun, sto korun). You'll run into this constantly with prices — „to stojí pět korun“ but „to stojí dvě koruny“. You don't need the grammar behind it yet (it's the genitive plural, covered properly in A2) — for now just listen for korun after any number five and above.

check.prompt: You want to ask a shop assistant the price of a jacket. What do you say?
check.explanation: „Kolik to stojí?“ is the standard way to ask how much something costs.
check.note: Pair it with „prosím“ to sound extra polite: „Kolik to stojí, prosím?“

check.prompt: „Tři koruny“ and „pět korun“ use the same ending for koruna.
check.explanation: They don't — 2–4 takes „koruny“, while 5 and above takes „korun“. Only 1 uses the plain form „koruna“.
check.note: This 1 / 2–4 / 5+ split shows up with every countable noun, not just koruna.

check.prompt: Ten telefon je moc ___. Nemám tolik peněz. (expensive)
check.explanation: Drahý means "expensive" — the opposite is levný ("cheap").
check.note: Drahý and levný are two of the most useful adjectives for any shopping conversation.

check.prompt: A male speaker makes his request more polite: „Chci ty boty.“ → „___ ty boty.“
check.explanation: Chci ("I want") is blunt; chtěl bych ("I would like") is the softer, more polite version a male speaker uses — chtěla bych for a female speaker.
check.note: Same softening pattern you've already seen for ordering food — it works the same way in shops.

title: Directions & places in town
blurb: Ask for and follow directions, and name the everyday places you'll need to find.

vocab.example: Pošta je blízko, jen pět minut pěšky.
Zastávka autobusu je na rohu ulice.

grammarNote.title: Giving directions: an early taste of the imperative
grammarNote.text: Directions are almost always given as commands, so you'll meet the imperative mood here before it's formally taught. For someone you'd address as vy, most verbs add -te: jít ("to go") → jděte, zahnout ("to turn") → zahněte. For someone you'd address as ty, drop the -te: jdi, zahni. You don't need the full conjugation rule yet — just recognize a -te verb at the start of a sentence as an instruction aimed at you.

check.prompt: Someone tells you „Zahněte doleva.“ What should you do?
check.explanation: Doleva means "left" (as a direction to turn). Doprava means "right".
check.note: Doleva and doprava look similar — the -leva/-prava part is the giveaway once you notice it.

check.explanation: „Rovně“ means "straight ahead", not "turn right" — that's doprava.
check.note: A very common beginner mix-up since rovně and doprava both start appearing in the same sentences.

check.prompt: Jděte ___ a pak zahněte doprava. (straight ahead)
check.explanation: Rovně is the word for "straight ahead" when giving directions.
check.note: This exact phrase pattern — jděte rovně a pak… — is worth memorizing whole.

check.prompt: Make it formal, for someone you'd address as vy: „Zahni doleva.“ → „___ doleva.“
check.explanation: The informal ty-command zahni becomes zahněte for vy — the same -te pattern as jdi → jděte.
check.note: Once you know one verb's ty/vy command pair, you can usually guess the pattern for others.

title: A1 review & mini-check
blurb: A light cumulative recap pulling together greetings, the verbs být/mít, gender, and everyday phrases from across A1.

vocab.translation: My name is… / What is your name? (formal)
vocab.example: Dobrý den, jmenuji se Petr. Jak se jmenujete?
Jsem z Indie a mám tady kamarády.
Kde bydlíte a proč jste v Praze?
Ten dům, ta kniha a to auto jsou moje.
Můj bratr a moje sestra bydlí v Brně.

grammarNote.title: Everything so far stays in the nominative — that changes next
grammarNote.text: Every sentence you've built in A1 has used nouns and adjectives in their plain dictionary form — the nominative case — and verbs only in the present tense. That's why „ten dům“, „moje sestra“, and „chtěl bych kávu“ all keep the noun unchanged no matter where it sits in the sentence. That stability ends in A2: the accusative case starts changing noun and adjective endings for direct objects (e.g. „Mám bratra“ instead of „Mám bratr“), so this is a good point to make sure the nominative forms and vocabulary here feel automatic before cases enter the picture.

check.prompt: You're meeting someone formally for the first time and want to ask their name. What do you say?
check.explanation: „Jak se jmenujete?“ is the formal way to ask someone's name.
check.note: Recap from Lesson 1 — the vy-form matches the formal register you'd use with a stranger.

check.prompt: „Máte“ is a form of mít ("to have"), used for vy.
check.explanation: Correct — máte is the vy-form of mít, just like máš is the ty-form.
check.note: Recap from the být & mít lesson — these two irregular verbs come up in almost every sentence.

check.prompt: ___ auto je nové. (that — auto is neuter)
check.explanation: Auto is a neuter noun, so it pairs with to, not ten or ta.
check.note: Recap from the nouns & gender lesson — spotting neuter nouns by their -o ending is a reliable shortcut.

check.prompt: Make it more polite: „Chci kávu.“ → „___ kávu.“
check.explanation: Chci is blunt; chtěl bych (male speaker) or chtěla bych (female speaker) is the polite version used when ordering.
check.note: Recap from the food & ordering lesson — this softening pattern also worked the same way for shopping.
